docs.D01_macro_context.md:
Title: What was known about international contagion on February 24
Source: compiled from: https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20200224-sitrep-35-covid-19.pdf; https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/84735/cdc_84735_DS1.pdf
Date: 2020-02-24

WHO Situation Report 35 gives data reported by 10am CET on February 24. Globally, 79,331 confirmed cases were reported, including 77,262 in China and 2,069 outside China. Outside-China cases were spread across 29 countries, with 300 new confirmed cases in the preceding reporting interval.

WHO reported 2,595 deaths in China and 23 outside China. The risk assessment was very high for China and high at regional and global levels. These are reported surveillance data, not an estimate of all infections or a prediction of eventual economic damage.

The January 30 CDC telebriefing had already announced person-to-person transmission in the United States between close household contacts. CDC also emphasized low risk to the general public in that setting. Both facts belong in the evidence: transmission was established, while authorities had not characterized all US communities as experiencing widespread uncontrolled infection.

By February 24, international clusters created a problem not confined to Chinese factory shutdowns. Restrictions, voluntary changes in behavior and uncertainty could affect travel, consumer activity and supply chains in multiple economies at once.

The investment question is not whether every eventual shutdown can be predicted. It is whether a sufficiently plausible severe interruption has a market price inconsistent with its potential impact on a concentrated portfolio.

Confirmed-case counts have reporting lags, testing limitations and differences across jurisdictions. A precise epidemiological model is not supplied. The documents do not infer an eventual infection fatality rate from the ratio of current deaths to current reported cases.

Neither a March pandemic declaration nor subsequent US lockdowns, central-bank programs, market lows or portfolio gains is included. The cutoff captures an emerging international threat with meaningful uncertainty, not a crisis whose full path is already known.

The favorable scenario remains containment, improved treatment/behavior and a limited interruption. The adverse scenario is a self-reinforcing contraction in mobility and spending accompanied by tighter financial conditions. A hedge decision must compare those possibilities with the cost, timing and basis risk of the proposed protection rather than assume the severe scenario is certain.
docs.D02_market_pricing.md:
Title: Equity repricing has started; exact credit execution levels remain unavailable
Source: compiled from: https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/24/us-futures-coronavirus-outbreak.html; https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/24/business/stock-market-coronavirus.html; https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/24/global-stocks-roiled-as-italy-and-south-korea-sound-coronavirus-alarm.html
Date: 2020-02-24

US markets sold off sharply on February 24 as cases outside China rose. CNBC reports the S&P 500 down 3.35% to 3,225.89, Nasdaq down 3.71% to 9,221.28 and the Dow down 1,031.61 points, or 3.56%, to 27,960.80.

The same report describes VIX increasing by more than seven points, roughly 46%, to about 25. This is the article's rounded contemporaneous observation, not a claim that a VIX option could be bought at that number.

The New York Times notes that the S&P had reached a record as recently as the preceding Wednesday and calls the decline the worst single-day performance since February 2018. It describes an abrupt change from earlier investor willingness to look past China's outbreak.

International evidence also matters. CNBC reports South Korea's Kospi down 3.9% and substantial Italian market weakness as new disease clusters raised fears. The repricing therefore spans countries rather than one company-specific earnings disappointment.

The exact February 24 CDX investment-grade, high-yield and iTraxx spreads, their bid/ask ranges, series and historical percentiles were not recovered from a dated source. No precise claim of record-tight spreads or a particular basis-point entry is made in the model-facing pack.

This is an important limitation, not a minor missing field. The attractiveness of credit protection depends on the executable spread, remaining tenor, upfront payment and coupon. A macro narrative alone cannot establish that the derivative offers favorable asymmetry.

Equity volatility has already risen, so put protection may be more expensive than before the day's decline. However, no option premium surface or direct cost comparison was recovered. Credit spreads and equity implied volatility are related risk prices, not substitutes with a fixed conversion.

The available evidence supports a live risk-management question: substantial uncertainty has become public, while equities remain near recently reached highs relative to a deep crisis scenario. It does not establish the precise hedge notional, fair spread or optimal execution time. Those require dealer terms and a portfolio stress model, neither of which is invented here.
docs.D03_instrument_economics.md:
Title: Credit-index protection mechanics and what can actually pay off
Source: https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1806b.htm
Date: 2018-06-05

The BIS June 2018 review describes major changes in the credit-default-swap market after the financial crisis, including smaller outstanding notionals and greater use of central clearing. It reports outstanding CDS notional declining from $61.2 trillion at end-2007 to $9.4 trillion ten years later.

A CDS protection buyer takes exposure to deterioration in reference credit risk while paying contractual consideration. An index references a defined basket of issuers. The trade can gain mark-to-market value as credit spreads widen before any constituent actually defaults.

That distinction matters for a portfolio hedge. The intended monetization need not wait for bankruptcies or full credit losses. If protection becomes more valuable during stress and can be closed at an attractive bid, it can create liquidity while long equity positions are impaired.

Economic premium, fixed coupon, upfront settlement, accrued interest and collateral are different quantities. Standardized contracts can combine coupons and upfront amounts; a quoted spread is not automatically equal to a simple annual cash premium. Exact documentation and dealer terms determine cash flows.

Notional is the reference amount, not the capital initially spent or the maximum plausible profit. Nor is it a directly comparable percentage of an equity portfolio. Credit duration, recovery assumptions, defaults, index composition and spread changes affect the payoff.

Spread sensitivity can be approximated locally using risky duration, but large shocks and defaults require a fuller valuation. Convexity is not free: protection can lose value through spread tightening and time/coupon payments if the adverse scenario does not arrive.

Central clearing changes counterparty exposure; it does not eliminate liquidity requirements, basis risk or all operational risks. Bilateral terms can create additional counterparty and collateral considerations. The pack does not assert that any specific proposed transaction is centrally cleared.

No dealer-confirmed index series, maturity, notional, upfront price, coupon or initial margin is supplied. The document is a mechanics reference available before 2020, not a term sheet. A decision should require explicit carry budgets, stress scenarios and close-out liquidity instead of treating the phrase “cheap insurance” as a complete instrument analysis.
docs.D04_portfolio_exposure.md:
Title: Why a concentrated quality-equity portfolio can still need liquidity insurance
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2020/02/03182429/Performance-Report-January-2020-PSH.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2019/08/20165951/PSH-2019-Interim-Financial-Statements1.pdf
Date: 2020-02-03

The January 31 portfolio update, published February 3, reports PSH assets/NAV of $5,582.6 million and total strategy assets/NAV of $7,019.2 million. The accompanying financial reporting identifies these as shareholder-capital measures. They are not a derivative notional or an estimate of cash ready to deploy.

The update reports total CDS exposure of zero at January month end. This does not establish the hedge book on February 24; it only identifies the latest recovered public observation.

The 2019 interim manager discussion covers concentrated positions in consumer, business-service and financial/industrial franchises, including Chipotle, Hilton, Lowe's, Restaurant Brands, ADP and Berkshire. This is a historical portfolio context, not a guarantee that all weights or holdings remain unchanged at the cutoff.

Those businesses have different revenue models, but a broad economic interruption can affect several simultaneously. Restaurants and hotels face mobility/consumer shocks, home improvement responds to household behavior, and a diversified insurer/industrial company still has market and operating exposures.

Owning strong long-run businesses does not remove short-run mark-to-market risk or create cash when other opportunities appear. A hedge may aim to protect purchasing power and avoid selling favored holdings into a disorderly market rather than express a permanent negative view on their intrinsic value.

The protection must nevertheless fit the actual risk. A diversified corporate credit index is not a precise hedge of a handful of equities. Credit issuers, geographies, duration and default exposure may differ substantially from the portfolio's consumer/operating sensitivities.

Exact current weights, cash, borrowing constraints, position-level stress losses and the manager-wide February NAV were not recovered. Consequently no optimal dollar notional or protection percentage is derived from the January NAV.

The relevant portfolio question is asymmetric liquidity: can a limited, affordable carrying cost produce useful cash in a severe common shock without forcing sales of high-quality holdings? That objective needs an explicit budget and exit discipline. It does not mean any amount of index protection is sensible, nor that a hedge should be retained indefinitely after risk is repriced.
docs.D05_alternatives.md:
Title: Comparing credit protection, equity puts and reducing exposure
Source: compiled from: https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1806b.htm; https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/24/us-futures-coronavirus-outbreak.html; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2020/02/03182429/Performance-Report-January-2020-PSH.pdf
Date: 2020-02-24

The main alternatives to credit-index protection are selling long positions, holding more cash, buying equity puts, reducing leverage or accepting the risk. They address different dimensions of the problem and should not be treated as economically identical.

Selling equities immediately removes exposure and raises cash without a recurring insurance premium. It may also crystallize taxes, forgo recoveries and require rebuilding concentrated stakes later. Those trade-offs depend on cost bases, valuation and portfolio constraints, which are not fully documented here.

Equity index puts more directly target an equity market decline but introduce strike, expiry and volatility pricing. February 24's large VIX move indicates that equity insurance pricing has changed; it does not quantify a particular put's cost or prove credit is cheaper on a risk-adjusted basis.

Credit-index protection offers a different stress exposure: wider spreads, defaults and increased credit risk can raise its value. It can be monetized before actual default if counterparties and market liquidity permit. The basis to the manager's actual equities remains material.

Reducing leverage can improve resilience without a derivative, but funding liabilities, asset sales and vehicle-specific capital arrangements matter. The January public NAV figures alone do not establish the exact leverage or debt-repayment opportunities available on February 24.

Doing nothing preserves full upside and avoids premium drag. That can be rational if risk is fairly priced or the portfolio already has adequate liquidity. It is less attractive if a small defined carrying cost can offset a plausible severe loss and create scarce reinvestment capital.

A proper comparison needs a common scenario set: contained outbreak, prolonged modest slowdown, synchronized recession and sharp financial disruption. For each, estimate equity losses, hedge gains/losses, cash flows, collateral and the time until payment.

No authentic dealer quotes for those alternatives were recovered, so no numeric “best hedge” ranking is supplied. The document sets out the decision dimensions, not a fabricated backtest or an outcome-based proof.

The central discipline is to buy exposure whose downside is affordable and whose stressed payoff is relevant. A convincing epidemic narrative is insufficient if the insurance is already expensive, the maturity wrong or the portfolio lacks the liquidity to carry it.
docs.D06_risks_falsifiers.md:
Title: What could make portfolio protection lose money or fail to protect
Source: compiled from: https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20200224-sitrep-35-covid-19.pdf; https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1806b.htm; https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/24/business/stock-market-coronavirus.html
Date: 2020-02-24

A protection buyer can be broadly correct about a serious disease and still make a poor investment. Timing, cost, tenor and payoff basis determine whether the instrument helps the portfolio.

Containment is a genuine alternative. WHO's high global risk assessment is not a deterministic forecast of a worldwide shutdown. Public-health intervention, changed behavior or limited onward transmission could reduce the economic tail without generating a large credit loss.

Credit spreads can tighten or remain stable while premiums accrue. Mark-to-market losses and coupon drag may occur before a severe scenario arrives, or the protection may expire before the relevant shock. An affordable monthly budget matters more than an impressive gross notional.

The equity/credit basis can also move unfavorably. Portfolio companies may face lower earnings and valuation multiples even if investment-grade borrowers remain solvent and credit markets stay liquid. Conversely, a credit-index spike may not match the size or duration of the portfolio drawdown.

Government or central-bank support could change credit pricing without immediately repairing underlying operating profits. A policy response can therefore reduce the hedge's prospective payoff while the manager still has weak long-equity marks.

Liquidity is another risk. A quoted theoretical value is not necessarily a bid at which a large position can be closed. Bid/ask spreads, collateral, counterparty arrangements and operational capacity affect monetization.

Falsifiers and decision checkpoints should be defined in advance: evidence of contained international transmission; restored mobility and activity; spreads already compensating for the severe scenario; excessive cumulative carry; or a portfolio whose own valuation has become sufficiently attractive to redeploy protection gains.

The exact thresholds cannot be calculated from the retrieved data because execution terms and a portfolio stress model are absent. They should be stated as required analysis rather than filled with invented numbers.

Nothing in this document uses later lockdowns, actual hedge gains or a later interview as evidence of foresight. The proposition is a bounded, probabilistic risk-management decision as of February 24. Conviction in the possibility of a shock is different from conviction that an unspecified derivative at an unspecified price is automatically attractive.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Public-information timeline through the first international repricing
Source: compiled from: https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/84735/cdc_84735_DS1.pdf; https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20200224-sitrep-35-covid-19.pdf; https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/24/business/stock-market-coronavirus.html; https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/24/global-stocks-roiled-as-italy-and-south-korea-sound-coronavirus-alarm.html
Date: 2020-02-24

**January 30:** CDC announces the first US person-to-person transmission in a close-contact household setting. Its telebriefing also emphasizes low general-public risk in that context. This is evidence of transmissibility, not evidence that a later US shutdown is already known.

**January 31 portfolio measurement:** The manager's public monthly update subsequently reports no CDS exposure at month end and strategy NAV of approximately $7.019 billion. It establishes a recent public baseline, not the exact book at inception of any subsequent trade.

**Early February:** Public attention focuses on the outbreak's Chinese economic impact and disruptions to activity. The retrieved February 24 press later describes investors as having previously looked past much of that threat. This is a dated contemporary characterization, not a hindsight claim that all markets were complacent.

**Week before February 24:** The S&P reaches a record on Wednesday, according to the February 24 New York Times account. The close proximity of a market high matters when assessing the range of possible drawdowns, but does not determine a fair credit spread.

**February 24 public-health update:** WHO reports 79,331 confirmed cases globally, 2,069 outside China and 29 affected countries outside China. Its global risk assessment is high. The report's measurement time is 10am CET, so it is not a final worldwide end-of-day tally.

**February 24 market session:** International clusters in Italy, South Korea and elsewhere drive broad risk repricing. The S&P falls 3.35%, the Dow 3.56% and Nasdaq 3.71%. Equity implied volatility rises substantially.

**Cutoff:** The pack permits end-of-day February 24 reporting. It does not claim these closing prices were available at an earlier intraday execution. Exact inception timing and CDS terms are unknown.

No March disclosure of the manager's hedge, television comments, policy rescue, monetization date or realized proceeds appears in the model-facing pack. Those are answer-key matters. The information set leaves a real decision: whether emerging international contagion and available risk prices justify a defined-cost protection overlay while preserving long-run equity ownership.

drivers.driver: Pandemic interruption risk was not adequately reflected in credit protection pricing.
Limited premiums offered an unusually asymmetric potential stress payoff.
Protect concentrated quality-equity holdings without forced liquidation.
Create liquidity to redeploy into attractive long investments when risk repriced.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: Seven hedge-specific documents. Primary WHO/CDC facts, dated market reports and portfolio NAV; exact credit spread/term-sheet data missing, a material gap. No invented notional, premium surface or future March information. Macro thesis codes are descriptive, not forced equity T/C categories.

final.risk: A pandemic-induced credit shock resulting in a self-reinforcing contraction in global mobility, consumer spending, and supply chains [D01].
final.market_implied_probability: Market is currently repricing risk as evidenced by a 3.35% drop in the S&P 500 and a ~46% increase in the VIX to ~25, but does not yet fully reflect a severe systemic credit crisis [D02].
final.our_probability_and_why: We believe there is an underpriced risk of a paradigm-shifting shock; while international clusters are emerging [D01], the market only recently transitioned from complacency [D02], and we view the probability of a severe economic interruption as sufficiently high to warrant protection [D01].
final.instrument: Credit default swaps (CDS) on investment-grade and high-yield indices [D03].
final.exit_rule: Monetize when the risk is clearly priced in or the threat passes, as indicated by a normalization of credit spreads or a change in the infectious disease trajectory [D03, D06].
final.memo:
On February 24, we face a shift from a localized Chinese supply-chain concern to a global pandemic risk with emerging clusters in Italy and South Korea [D01, D07]. Despite the sharp equity market decline, the potential for a self-reinforcing contraction remains a paradigm-shifting threat that is not yet fully discounted by the credit markets [D01, D02].

Our objective is to secure asymmetric liquidity [D04]. By purchasing protection through credit-index CDS, we aim to offset potential portfolio impairments and generate reinvestment capital without liquidating our high-quality, long-term holdings [D03, D04]. We accept a limited, defined premium to protect against a scenario that the market currently misprices as low-probability, maintaining our discipline to exit once the asymmetry is realized or extinguished [D06].

final.risk: A pandemic-induced, self-reinforcing contraction in global mobility, consumer spending, and supply chains leading to a severe credit and economic shock [D01].
final.market_implied_probability: While specific credit spread levels are not in the pack, equity markets have begun to reprice with a 3.35% drop in the S&P 500 and a ~46% increase in the VIX [D02].
final.our_probability_and_why: We assign a high enough probability to a severe economic interruption to justify hedging, as current international clusters in Italy and South Korea signal that the risk is no longer confined to China [D01, D07]. The market previously looked past the outbreak; the recent spike in volatility suggests a paradigm-shifting risk is now becoming visible but may not yet fully reflect the potential for a systemic credit event [D02].
final.instrument: Credit default swaps (CDS) on investment-grade and high-yield credit indices [D03].
final.exit_rule: Monetize when credit spreads reach levels that adequately compensate for the stressed economic scenario or when the fundamental risk of a systemic shutdown has passed [D06].
final.memo:
As of February 24, we are observing an abrupt transition in market sentiment as international contagion becomes apparent [D02]. While our portfolio remains concentrated in high-quality, free-cash-flow-generative businesses, a broad economic shock—characterized by a self-reinforcing contraction in mobility and consumption—poses a meaningful threat to short-term liquidity [D01, D04]. Our discipline is to protect the portfolio against paradigm-shifting risks that the market is only beginning to price, using instruments that provide asymmetric payoffs [D04, D06].

We favor CDS protection because it offers a direct way to capitalize on the widening of credit spreads that would accompany a systemic financial shock [D03, D05]. Unlike selling our long-term holdings, which would crystallize losses and force us to exit positions in high-quality compounders, a credit hedge allows us to generate liquidity precisely when other opportunities might arise [D04, D05]. We acknowledge the uncertainty regarding exact entry spreads and liquidity; therefore, our commitment is limited to a defined premium that keeps our carrying cost affordable while providing significant upside in the event of a market dislocation [D02, D06].
